Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Case Vignette for Thomas Thomas, a 21-year-old European male and public defender, recently sought help after experiencing escalating symptoms following his traumatic experience as a refugee. Born in Eastern Europe, Thomas fled with his family during a period of violent conflict that left deep scars on his psyche. At the time, he was only 14 years old when they were caught in the crossfire of an attack on their small village. Thomas vividly remembers the chaos and fear that engulfed him as bullets whizzed past them and explosions echoed through the night air. His family managed to escape by hiding for days before finally crossing the border into safety. However, those harrowing moments have left indelible marks in his mind, manifesting in various symptoms of PTSD. Since arriving in America, Thomas has struggled with constant thoughts about the event. He often finds himself monitoring his own thoughts for signs that he is "going crazy." This internal vigilance makes it difficult for him to engage fully in conversations or activities outside of work. When he does talk about the event, even in therapy sessions, he feels incredibly uncomfortable and tries to change the subject as quickly as possible. Thomas avoids situations where he might be reminded of his traumatic experience. For example, he becomes extremely anxious if someone brings up similar stories or discusses events that remind him of his past. This avoidance extends to his interactions with colleagues at work; he often withdraws from conversations about cases involving refugees or conflict zones, fearing the memories and feelings it may trigger. The startle response has become a significant issue for Thomas. Ordinary sounds—such as sudden door slams or loud voices—often cause him to jump or react with fear. He is always on edge, convinced that something dangerous is lurking around every corner. The silence can be even more unsettling; when there’s an unusual quiet, he feels an intense sense of foreboding, believing that danger is imminent. Thomas experiences intrusive memories and bodily reenactments frequently. Sometimes, vivid visual images flash in his mind, bringing him back to the village under attack. At other times, he feels physically as if he were still hiding or running from danger, with a racing heart and tense muscles. These episodes can occur without any clear trigger, leaving him feeling overwhelmed by intense emotions such as fear and helplessness. Thomas’s negative appraisals are deeply ingrained in his worldview. He believes that the world is an inherently dangerous place where he must remain hypervigilant at all times. His constant vigilance has made it difficult to relax or trust others, creating a sense of isolation even within his relationship with his girlfriend. The fear that something terrible could happen again at any moment has taken its toll on both his personal and professional life. Over the past few months, these symptoms have gradually intensified, affecting his ability to focus on his work as a public defender. He finds it increasingly challenging to maintain relationships and engage in daily activities without feeling constantly anxious or overwhelmed by memories of the traumatic event. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was a recent incident where he had a panic attack during a court hearing. His girlfriend also expressed growing concerns about how his symptoms were affecting their relationship, urging him to get professional support. Thomas is most afraid that he will never be able to escape the grip of these memories and constant fear. However, he is also hopeful that with therapy, he can learn strategies to manage his symptoms and regain a sense of control over his life. He wants to reconnect with people around him and live without the constant dread of danger lurking in every moment.
